chunks: From him, from Al-Fadl and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, all together, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Zurara, who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): A man entered with a group in their prayer, while he did not intend it to be a prayer. Then their Imam broke his ablution, so he took the hand of that man and brought him forward, so he led them in prayer. Would their prayer be sufficient by his prayer, while he did not intend it to be a prayer? He (peace be upon him) said: It is not befitting for the man that he enters with a group in their prayer while he does not intend it to be a prayer, but it is befitting for him that he intends it to be a prayer. If he had already prayed, then he has another prayer, otherwise he should not enter with them. Their prayer would suffice for the group, even if he did not intend it.
Their prayer would suffice for the group, even if he did not intend it.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a man joining a prayer without intending it as a prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the fiqh of joining a congregational prayer (Salat al-Jama'ah) without prior specific intention, ruling that the Imam (peace be upon him) validates the congregation's prayer even if the latecomer does not intend it as a distinct obligatory act. It establishes that if the individual has already fulfilled their duty, the late entry serves as supererogatory (Nafl), whereas if not, they must intend it to be valid. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the flexibility of niyyah in communal settings, prioritizing the unity of the congregation over rigid individual intentionality for the latecomer.
